item.title: New Zealand Men’s 7s Development Team returns to Coral Coast 7s eyeing historic title
item.description: The Men in Black are coming back to Rugbytown, with the goal of winning it all. The New Zealand Men's 7s Development Team has confirmed its return to the 2027 McDonald's Coral Coast Fiji 7s, bringing with it a mission that no overseas team has accomplished in the tournament's history: winning the prestigious i-Wau Trophy.
item.content:encoded:
The Men in Black are coming back to Rugbytown, with the goal of winning it all.

The New Zealand Men's 7s Development Team has confirmed its return to the 2027 McDonald's Coral Coast Fiji 7s, bringing with it a mission that no overseas team has accomplished in the tournament's history: winning the prestigious i-Wau Trophy.

While international teams have travelled to Fiji over the years with impressive credentials and talented squads, the i-Wau Trophy has remained firmly in Fijian hands.

New Zealand's development squad will be out to change that.

The New Zealand side returns to Sigatoka for valuable international experience that prepares players for the demands of elite sevens rugby.

Equally the team’s objective is to become the first overseas team to win the McDonald's Coral Coast Fiji 7s.

With New Zealand's established reputation as one of the world's leading rugby sevens nations, the development squad is expected to bring a combination of emerging talent, athleticism and the disciplined playing style associated with the famous black jersey.

But success on Fijian soil will be anything but straightforward.

The Coral Coast Fiji 7s has earned a reputation for its fiercely competitive environment, where established international teams regularly find themselves challenged by Fiji's outstanding grassroots talent.

For the New Zealanders, winning the i-Wau Trophy would represent a significant achievement and a historic breakthrough for overseas participation in the tournament.

Tournament Chairman Jay Whyte welcomed the return of the New Zealand Men's Development Team and their ambition to rewrite the tournament's history.

Whyte says he loves the fact that the New Zealanders are playing to win.

He says they are not coming to Sigatoka for a holiday, they are coming with a purpose, and that purpose is to take the i-Wau Trophy back across the Pacific.

The Tournament Chairman says there is one rather significant obstacle standing in their way.

He says in 14 previous editions, no overseas team has ever managed to win the men's championship.

Whyte says some outstanding international teams have tried, and every single time the trophy has remained here in Fiji.

The 15th annual tournament, scheduled for 14–16 January 2027 at Lawaqa Park, Sigatoka, will feature 24 men's teams competing for the championship and a FJD $50,000 first prize.

item.title: Nadi sprint stars eye double gold at Tuckers games
item.description: Twelve-year-old Tevita Naivalu hopes to add another gold medal to Nadi's tally today as he competes in the Under-13 Boys' 200m final, after winning the 100m race yesterday. Naivalu sprinted to victory in his 200m heat this morning, securing his place in the final as he looks to strike gold once again for Nadi.
item.content:encoded:
Twelve-year-old Tevita Naivalu hopes to add another gold medal to Nadi's tally today as he competes in the Under-13 Boys' 200m final, after winning the 100m race yesterday.

Naivalu sprinted to victory in his 200m heat this morning, securing his place in the final as he looks to strike gold once again for Nadi.

Naivalu also represented Fiji in the Pacific Mini Games.

Meanwhile, Mereoni Levula of Nadi is also chasing her second gold medal in the Under-13 Girls' 200m event at the Fiji Tuckers Ice Cream School Games.

Levula, a rising talent from Nadi, claimed gold in the 100m event yesterday.

She is no stranger to the track, having been a consistent performer since the Under-10 grade.

Western schools have been showing strong performances in the 200m heats in both the boys' and girls' divisions however, Serua dominated the boys' 200m heats, setting the stage for an exciting final this afternoon.

All eyes will now be on the young athletes as they compete for gold in the finals scheduled for after lunch.

Stay with us for more updates from the Fiji Tuckers Ice Cream School Games.

item.title: Those who washed dirty boots and prepared meals honoured at SGS capping
item.description: Those who washed dirty boots and clothes, prepared meals and made financial sacrifices to support Suva Grammar School's Under-18 rugby players were among those honoured during the school's capping ceremony. Suva Grammar School Principal Iosefo Masivue dedicated the ceremony to every parent, guardian and supporter who stood behind the players throughout the rugby season.
item.content:encoded:
Those who washed dirty boots and clothes, prepared meals and made financial sacrifices to support Suva Grammar School's Under-18 rugby players were among those honoured during the school's capping ceremony.

Suva Grammar School Principal Iosefo Masivue dedicated the ceremony to every parent, guardian and supporter who stood behind the players throughout the rugby season.

Masivue says winning three Deans titles was the pinnacle of the school's achievements this year, marking the end of a 21-year wait to finally lift the Vodafone Super Deans Trophy.

However, he reminded the players that beyond the trophies and victories, what truly mattered was the humanity, discipline and character they had developed throughout the rugby season.

He emphasised that the capping ceremony was not just about recognising the players, but also honouring the people who had made their journey possible.

He says the caps belonged to everyone who had supported the boys behind the scenes, from parents who washed their dirty boots and clothes to those who prepared their lunches, provided financial assistance and made sacrifices for the players' welfare.

Masivue also dedicated the historic victory to the late coach Peli Osborne, acknowledging the years he had spent grooming and developing students into champions.

He reminded the newly capped players of three important responsibilities: to remember those who came before them and paved the way for their success, to consider those who would follow in their footsteps, and, most importantly, to remember who they represented.

He urged the boys to carry the school's name with pride, dignity and respect.

His transition from playing as a winger to taking on the role of hooker in the Under-18 team highlighted his versatility, commitment and development as a rugby player.
